declarations.documentation:
Serve a channel forever, delivering each incoming message to @deliver_to@ as one `message` value —
shaped like `time.watch` / `google_calendar.watch` so it composes under `parallel [ … ]`. The bot's own
posts (and other bots') are not delivered, so replying from @deliver_to@ cannot loop.

Delivery is at-least-once while this call is running: Slack re-sends an event whose acknowledgement was
lost to a dropped socket, so a message can be repeated but not missed, and no dedup memory is kept here.
A message posted while the watch is down is never delivered at all, so a bot that must reconcile that gap
keeps the `id` of the last message it handled somewhere durable and closes the gap with `list_messages`.

The Socket Mode connection belongs to this call (shared with any other live watch or `ask` on the same
app-level token) and dies with it — and the watch supervises itself: a panic, which is how a runtime
restart interrupts the call under the at-most-once rule, reopens the connection with freshly resolved
credentials, on an exponential backoff capped at fifteen minutes. A typed `slack_error` still flies:
`auth_error` for a bad app-level token stops the watch loudly rather than retrying into a locked door,
`api_error` for a transient network fault at open. The mortal single-connection form is `slack_watch`.

declarations.documentation:
The gap reader: a channel's own messages posted after @after@, in posted order — the reconciliation
`watch_messages` tells you to write, since Socket Mode delivers only to a running watch. @after@ is a
message `ts`, not a wall clock: hand back the `id` of the last message you handled (kept durably — a
`var` dies with the run) and everything posted since arrives oldest first, ready for the same handling
the watch would have run. An empty @after@ reads the newest @limit@ instead, which is the shape for a
first run with no cursor yet.

The answer is the same `message` value the watch delivers, attachments downloaded into `file` values and
bot posts dropped, so one handler serves both paths — a page of image-heavy history pays for every
attachment on it, so keep @limit@ to what you will actually process. @limit@ is clamped into 1-200, so a wide gap takes
several calls, and only an empty answer means it is closed — dropped bot posts and skipped subtypes
shorten a page too. Nothing here dedups. Raises `slack_error` exactly as `send_message` does, and it
needs the `channels:history` (or `groups:history`) scope, which watching a channel does not by itself
grant.

declarations.documentation:
Post @prompt@ with @controls@ under it and block until someone in the channel answers, returning the
`answer` that control produced. It is the one interaction primitive, so the four human-in-the-loop shapes
are four control lists rather than four agents: an approval is two `button`s, an open question a one-field
`form`, a draft review a `form` whose `field` is prefilled with the draft, and a multiple choice a
`select`. Every control is live at once and the first answer settles the ask; the controls are then
stripped from the message, so a second answer has nothing to press. Branch on the control's own id —
`case clicked(id => "approve", by => _)` — never on display text.

The channel's membership is the trust boundary: any member may answer, and @by@ on the answer is the
answerer's raw Slack user id, so pass it through `crypto.pseudonym` before letting it leave the program.
Opening a `form`'s dialog and closing it again is not an answer, so a curious press cannot consume the
ask. A `form`'s inputs are not validated at all, and cannot be: the socket acknowledges every interaction
the instant it arrives, which is exactly what closes the dialog, so per-field errors can never be
returned. Validate in the program and `ask` again.

The ask holds no time limit: a deadline is `time.with_deadline` wrapped around it, a withdrawal is
`region.cancel_by_id` on the fiber holding it. Every ending takes the controls off, best-effort and
fire-and-forget — an answer leaves its own outcome line, a cancel or expired deadline leaves `(expired)`,
a question the platform broke leaves `(failed)`. One ending cannot: a runtime restart interrupts the call
under the at-most-once rule and takes the prompt's identity with it, so let the panic ride to your
supervisor and ask again.

Nothing here is clamped: a string past one of the numbers `limits` publishes is Slack's rejection arriving
as a typed `api_error`, and a form's own caps show when its dialog opens rather than when the question
posts. Run `check_controls` where the controls are built — it is deliberately not wired in here, since
`ask` returns an `answer` with no room for a verdict and what a failed check means is the caller's
decision. A control portable to the Discord twin takes the tighter of the two platforms' numbers: a
≤24-character title, ≤45-character field labels, ≤75-character button labels and options. Raises
`slack_error` when a Slack call fails; catch `api_error` to ask again.

declarations.documentation:
Check @controls@ against Slack's caps locally and answer with a value — `valid`, or `invalid` carrying
one sentence naming the offending control. Pure: no connection, no io, nothing to catch, so it belongs
where the controls are built (a gate's constructor, a test) rather than where they are asked. It is
deliberately not wired into `ask`, which returns an `answer` with no room for a verdict; a caller must be
free to decide what a failed check means.

It reports every string blank or past its cap in `limits`, every count (including an empty @controls@,
which Slack posts happily as a bare prompt that nobody can ever answer, so the ask waits forever), and
duplicate ids — two controls sharing an `action_id` cannot be told apart on the way back, so a press on
one would answer as the other, and a `form`'s @fields@ are checked the same way, since `submitted.values`
is keyed by field id.
